 Home Sports NZ vs India | 29/3 in Wellington Brings Back an Uncomfortable 2018 Echo NZ vs India | 29/3 in Wellington Brings Back an Uncomfortable 2018 Echo
 Rajiv Singh Last Updated: November 7, 2026, 09:48 IST Summarise Share Share New Zealand know how to make visiting batters uncomfortable against a moving ball. In Wellington, India turned that examination on the hosts, restricting them to a start that belongs alongside some of their leanest opening 10 overs at home Tim Seifert fell for a five-ball duck, caught by Anshul Kamboj off Auqib Nabi, as India restricted New Zealand to 29/3 after 10 overs in the second ODI in Wellington   Credits: ANI New Zealand had scored 23 runs in nine overs. Daryl Mitchell then hit a six. Five dot balls completed the 10th, and the scoreboard settled at 29/3.
 It was a small burst of defiance inside an opening spell controlled by India. The six supplied more than a fifth of New Zealand’s runs. Around it, the hosts had struggled to find even the modest scoring rhythm that keeps an innings from becoming an exercise in survival.

This was Wellington, with swing and seam asking questions New Zealand’s batters have spent their careers answering. The home advantage should have included an understanding of those questions. Instead, India’s bowlers were setting them, and New Zealand’s top order had already failed three.

 The company that 29/3 keeps
 The immediate historical echo comes from Hamilton on February 25, 2018. Against England, New Zealand finished their first 10 overs at 28/3. Wellington produced an almost identical opening score eight years later.
 Recommended Stories EXPLAINED | ‘Clicky Ponting’ Scandal: How a Finger Snap Fooled a Cricket Umpire "Bharat's Daughter Scripts History": Sports Minister Congratulates Tanvi Patri on Youth Olympics Silver "Second BWF Title of the Season": Kiren Rijiju Congratulates PV Sindhu on HYLO Open 2026 Triumph "We Stuck to Our Plan for 60 Minutes": Harmanpreet After India Clinch Record 6th Asian Champions Trophy Michael Hussey Joins Australia’s Coaching Staff for 2027 Ashes and World Cup But Hamilton is one point in a broader history of uncomfortable home starts.
 Against England in Auckland on February 23, 2013, New Zealand managed 18/3 after 10 overs. Three days earlier, they had reached just 21/2 in Napier. West Indies restricted them to 20/3 at Eden Park on Boxing Day that year. England held them to 27/2 in Christchurch in March 2018. Bangladesh produced another 27/2 in Napier in December 2023.
 These examples place Wellington among New Zealand’s leanest opening passages at home. They also expose the weakness in reading the run total alone.
 Twenty-seven for two and 29/3 are separated by two runs. The additional wicket carries a much larger cost. It brings another batter to the crease against an attack already controlling the scoring, while reducing the side’s capacity to take risks. A slow start becomes harder to correct when each attempted release threatens to deepen the damage.
 Wellington combined both problems. New Zealand were scoring below three an over and had already lost their top three.
 Familiarity has to survive the first spell
 Home advantage is often discussed through the discomfort of the visitor. Touring batters must adjust to the bounce, the movement and the lengths that demand a response.
 Wellington reversed that familiar conversation.
 New Zealand’s batters had the experience of local conditions. India’s seamers had the immediate advantage of making the ball misbehave. The contest still depended on what happened between release and contact. A batter’s familiarity with swing offers limited comfort if the bowler can keep threatening the edge or the stumps.
 The dismissals showed India reaching both.
 Will Young was caught behind off Nabi. Nicholls was bowled by Kamboj. Seifert had already fallen to Nabi without scoring. India had found a way through each of the first three batters before New Zealand could establish a platform.
 The hosts’ problem extended beyond those wicket balls. Seifert faced five deliveries, Young 17 and Nicholls 26. Those stays yielded zero, six and 11. Time at the crease was accumulating without enough runs to transfer pressure back to the bowlers.
 That allowed India to keep asking the same questions.
 England’s 2013 lesson
 The Auckland example from 2013 shows how severe that squeeze can become.
 Steven Finn and James Anderson shared the first three wickets. Finn removed openers BJ Watling and Hamish Rutherford, while Anderson dismissed Kane Williamson. Their opening five-over spells cost six and 12 runs respectively. New Zealand finished the first 10 overs at 18/3.
 Eden Park’s short boundaries had offered the prospect of runs. England’s accuracy and penetration denied New Zealand the opportunity to exploit them.
 In Napier earlier that week, Anderson had bowled into a strong easterly wind as England restricted the hosts to 21/2 after 10 overs. The assistance available to a bowler still had to be used through control of line and length. England did that well enough to make New Zealand struggle across successive matches.
 Those examples give Wellington its context. Conditions can encourage a seam attack. The scoreboard measures how effectively that encouragement has been converted into pressure.
 India made the pressure count
 Mitchell’s six in the 10th over briefly interrupted that pressure. The five dots around it showed how firmly it remained in place. Nabi completed his first five overs with 2/21, having removed both openers.
 New Zealand had scored fewer runs after 10 overs on several previous occasions at home. Wellington’s particular sting lay in the combination of a sub-30 total, three wickets lost and familiar conditions mastered by the visiting attack.
 Sixty legal deliveries were enough to overturn the comfortable assumption that the home batters would be better equipped for the moving ball. New Zealand knew the conditions. India made them count.
